title: One Story, Four Retellings
objective: Compare how the approved sources retell the Christmas nativity, record two details that appear in only one of them, and explain in one sentence what a retelling emphasises by what it leaves out.

blocks.text: GROW · Humanities · Week 5. RE and World Views. One Story, Four Retellings.

Objective: compare how the approved sources retell the Christmas nativity, record two details that appear in only one of them, and explain in one sentence what a retelling emphasises by what it leaves out.
Success evidence: two details recorded with the source they appear in, and one sentence on what a retelling emphasises by leaving something out.
Everything comes from the approved source cards. You report what each source says; nobody is asked what they believe.
40 minutes. Offline.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve

blocks.text: A retelling is a set of choices
Nobody who retells a story tells all of it. There is never time.
What gets kept and what gets left out is a choice, even when nobody notices making it.
Comparing two retellings shows you those choices from the outside.
That is a skill you use in every subject, not only this one.
Today the story is the nativity and there are four sources on the sheet.
Keep the comparison between the sources on the sheet. Do not ask the room what they were taught at home.
You need the four source cards, the comparison grid and the record sheet.

stages.data-ta1: Source cards laid out in order before the lesson opens; the grid comes out after the first reading.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil says a source is wrong, ask which source they are comparing it with, and record both.

blocks.text: Two accounts of the same arrival
Source one has shepherds in it and no wise men.
Source two has wise men in it and no shepherds.
A lot of people would say both, because that is how the story is usually told now.
The combined version is a fifth retelling, made later, and it is not on your sheet.
Noticing that is the whole skill: what you thought was the story is one telling of it.

items: 1 · read one source at a time.

stages.title: I Do · model

blocks.text: Building the grid one source at a time
I read source one and list what is in it: shepherds, a manger, an angel.
I do not compare yet. Comparing while reading makes you see what you expect.
Then source two: wise men, a star, gifts, a journey.
Now I put the two lists side by side and look for what appears once.
The star is in source two only. The shepherds are in source one only.

blocks.caption: Comparing while reading makes you find what you expected
blocks.title: Comparing two retellings
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: read and list the first, read and list the second, compare, name what appears once

blocks.text: Then the harder question: what does source one emphasise by leaving the star out?
It puts ordinary working people at the centre of the arrival, and nobody grand.
Make the emphasis sentence the last thing, and say why it could not have come first.

stages.data-ta1: Model reading one source completely before opening the second. The order is the technique.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits

blocks.text: Sort the details
Six detail cards are on your table. Sort them into in more than one source and in only one.
A manger. A star. Shepherds. An angel. Gifts. A journey from far away.
Then match each in-only-one card to the source it appears in.
When your table is done, hold up the one you were least sure about.

stages.data-ta1: Cards sorted first. Nobody holds anything up until every table has finished.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect

blocks.text: Leaving out is a way of pointing
What a retelling leaves out shapes what a listener notices as much as what it puts in.
Take the wise men out and the arrival happens among people with no power at all.
Take the shepherds out and the arrival is recognised by learned travellers from elsewhere.
Neither telling says the other is false. Each one points somewhere.

blocks.caption: The same event, pointed two ways
blocks.title: Emphasis by omission
blocks.alt: Two boxes compared: what a retelling keeps and what it leaves out, and where each points

blocks.text: So your sentence names what is left out and says what that makes the reader notice.
Write it about the source, not about whether the story is true.

stages.data-ta1: Both source cards visible while pupils write the emphasis sentence.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab

blocks.text: Name the source from the detail
Work in twos. Read your partner one detail from your sheet.
They say which source it comes from.
If they cannot, check whether the detail is actually in more than one.
A detail in two sources is not evidence of a choice.
Then swap over and do the same for theirs.

stages.data-ta1: Pair by table. Two and a half minutes each way, timed aloud.

stages.title: Independent · evidence

blocks.text: Two details and one sentence
Work on your own. Read each source completely before comparing.
Record two details that appear in only one source, and name the source for each.
Then write one sentence on what a source emphasises by what it leaves out.
Write about the source's choices, not about whether the events happened.
If you finish early, name a detail the modern combined version adds to both.

items: Supported · one detail with its source, and the sentence said aloud.
Standard · two details with sources, and a written sentence on emphasis.
Stretch · as Standard, and name a detail the modern combined version adds.

stages.data-ta1: Scribe exactly. Do not correct a pupil's wording into the card's.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who wants to write about their own tradition may do so on the back; it is not marked.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence

blocks.text: Read the emphasis sentence to an adult
Read your sentence to the adult at your table.
They read it back and name the source they think it is about.
If they name the wrong one, add the source into the sentence and read it again.
Then choose what happens next: keep the sheet, add a third detail, or compare a third source.
Write the choice on the sheet with today's date before you leave.

stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads it back word for word and names the source they hear.

sections: What appears once, and what that emphasises
print.intro: Use one row per detail, with its source beside it. Leave a row blank rather than recording a detail you cannot place.
focusRows: Two details that appear in only one source
The source named for each detail

tiers: Record one detail with its source and say the sentence aloud.
Record two details with sources and write the sentence on emphasis.
As Standard, and name a detail the modern combined version adds.
checks: Each source was read completely before any comparison was made.
Every detail names the source it appears in.
The sentence is about the source's choices, not about whether the events happened.
No pupil was asked what they or their family believe.
